title: Noah Goodhart
text: Hello there! My name is Noah Goodhart and I am currently a senior in the Ecosystem Science and Sustainability major at Colorado State University. I am a Colorado native, and in my free time I love to ski and fly kites. I want to pursue a career in sustainability or hydrology ideally at a ski resort in Colorado, because skiing was such an integral part of my upbringing, and I want to make sure future generations have the same opportunity.

title: CSU Projects
text:
In the Spring of 2025 I took a class Quantative Reasoning class based in R. I wrote some code, and did some cool data science. Here is a collection of links!
Visit My Quarto Website
In this project, I learned the basics of building a Quarto website. Tasks I learned included committing and pushing edits, navigating GitHub, creating new .qmd files to add to my website, creating links, uploading pdfs, correcting my YAML formatting, and editting my .yml file to change the cosmetics of my website.
Lab 2
In this lab, I utilized the dplyr package in R to analyze a comprehensive dataset of tree growth from Minnesota, spanning 1897 to 2007. The dataset included annual radial growth increments for over 2,000 trees across various species and stands. Through this project, I applied data manipulation techniques such as filtering, slicing, arranging, and summarizing to explore patterns in tree growth. I also calculated derived metrics like diameter at breast height (DBH) and basal area, and classified trees based on DBH categories. This hands-on experience enhanced my proficiency in data wrangling and provided insights into how climate factors influence forest dynamics over time.

Lab 3
In Lab 3 of ESS 330, I engaged in data wrangling and visualization using real-world COVID-19 data from the New York Times. I filtered the dataset to focus on Colorado counties, calculated daily new cases and deaths, and identified counties with the highest cumulative and new case counts as of February 1, 2022. By integrating population data, I normalized case numbers to assess per capita impacts across counties. This exercise enhanced my proficiency in data manipulation with R and deepened my understanding of how to interpret and communicate public health data effectively.

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("lab3pic.png")) 








Lab 4
In Lab 4 of ESS 330, I engaged in statistical analysis using R to examine ecological data from the Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) Network, focusing on vertebrate species in Oregon’s Mack Creek. I applied univariate and bivariate statistical tests, including chi-square tests for categorical variables, t-tests for comparing means, and correlation analyses to explore relationships between variables. Additionally, I conducted multivariate analyses such as ANOVA and multiple linear regression to assess the influence of forest treatment types (clear-cut vs. old-growth) on species characteristics like length and weight. This lab enhanced my proficiency in R and deepened my understanding of applying statistical methods to real-world ecological data.

Lab 5
For this lab, we were required to create 2 project proposals each, that we would later refine and eventually choose one to work on for our final project. For each proposal, we had to include a title, justification explaining the significance of the project with supporting background information, with the specific objective that we would aim to achieve in this study and a testable hypothesis, model or analysis we would want to carry out. We also had to include our proposed methods where we briefly described how we planed to carry out our study, and our expected outcomes.

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("lab5pic.png")) 








Lab 6
In Lab 6 of ESS 330, I explored predictive modeling in hydrology using the tidymodels framework in R and the CAMELS (Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies) dataset. This lab involved building machine learning models to predict mean streamflow for various U.S. river basins based on their physical and climatic characteristics. Through this process, I gained hands-on experience in data preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and validation, enhancing my understanding of applying machine learning techniques to real-world environmental data.

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("lab6pic.png")) 








Lab 7
In this lab, we decided on a topic for our final project. We decided to test ENSO-Drought Linkages in Colorado. We wanted to see if ENSO types, (El Niño and La Niña) were an accurate way to predict droughts in Colorado. We took precipitation data from all of Colorado, and also drought data from all of Colorado. We then averaged these data points into one month, and then created 3-month rolling averages to match up with the ENSO severity data.

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("lab7pic.png")) 








Lab 8
In Lab 8 of ESS 330, I built upon the predictive modeling skills developed in Lab 6 by creating a complete machine learning pipeline using the tidymodels framework in R. Focusing on the CAMELS dataset, I aimed to predict mean streamflow (q_mean) for various U.S. river basins based on their physical and climatic characteristics. The process involved data cleaning, feature engineering, and splitting the dataset into training and testing sets. I then defined three candidate models—such as linear regression, random forest, and gradient boosting—and evaluated their performance using 10-fold cross-validation. After selecting the best-performing model, I fine-tuned its hyperparameters to optimize predictive accuracy. Finally, I visualized the model’s predictions spatially by mapping them across the river basins. This lab enhanced my understanding of the end-to-end machine learning workflow and its application to real-world hydrological data.
Lab 9
In Lab 9 of ESS 330, I collaborated with my peers to investigate the relationship between the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and drought conditions across Colorado counties. Utilizing datasets such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), U.S. Drought Monitor classifications, and the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), we conducted statistical analyses using R. Our approach included data preprocessing to align temporal scales, calculating Pearson correlation coefficients, and visualizing relationships through scatter plots with linear regression lines. This project enhanced my skills in data analysis and visualization, and deepened my understanding of how large-scale climate patterns like ENSO can influence regional drought conditions.

Lab 10
In Lab 10 of ESS 330, I explored spatial data analysis using R, focusing on calculating distances between geographic features and understanding coordinate reference systems (CRS). I utilized the sf package to work with spatial objects, transforming geometries into an Equidistant Conic projection to ensure accurate distance measurements across the continental United States. The lab involved importing datasets for U.S. states, neighboring countries, and U.S. cities, and computing distances from each city to the nearest U.S. border, state boundary, Mexico, and Canada. Through this exercise, I enhanced my skills in spatial data manipulation, CRS transformations, and geospatial visualization using ggplot2, gaining a deeper understanding of how spatial relationships can be quantified and represented in ecological studies.

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("lab10pic.png")) 








Final Report
In our final project for ESS 330, my group and I investigated the relationship between the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and drought severity across five Colorado counties: Kit Carson, Costilla, Larimer, Mesa, and Park. Utilizing R, we analyzed datasets including the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and the Drought Severity and Coverage Index (DSCI) to assess correlations between ENSO phases and drought conditions. Our findings revealed a weak to moderate negative correlation between ENSO severity and SPI in most counties, with Costilla County being an exception. The DSCI showed little to no statistically significant correlation across all counties, suggesting that ENSO may have limited predictive power for drought severity during its specific cycle. This challenges the common assumption that El Niño events increase precipitation in Colorado. We also observed a potential temporal lag between ENSO phases and drought conditions, indicating that future studies could benefit from lagged time-series modeling. This project enhanced my skills in data analysis and deepened my understanding of the complex interactions between large-scale climate patterns and regional drought conditions.
